# Assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell

## The Victim: George Lincoln Rockwell and the American Nazi Party

George Lincoln Rockwell was a prominent and controversial figure in the American far-right movement during the mid-20th century . He founded the American Nazi Party (ANP) in March 1959 in Arlington, Virginia, establishing it as a significant, albeit small, presence in the national political landscape , . At the time of his death in August 1967, the party had an estimated nationwide membership of under 1,000 individuals . Despite its relatively small size, the ANP, under Rockwell's leadership, gained notoriety through public rallies, media outreach, and overt political activism . Rockwell ran for president in 1964, using the platform to advance his extremist views . The party's stated goals included policies aimed at racial extermination and segregation, such as killing all Jews and sending Black people to Africa . While his rhetoric was explicitly genocidal, his approach to achieving these ends was more public-facing than that of later, more clandestine factions. Rockwell engaged with the mainstream political system, even participating in public debates; for instance, he gave a speech at Wisconsin State University-Eau Claire on February 16, 1967, invited jointly by the College Republicans and College Democrats .

Rockwell's ideology, while rooted in Nazism, incorporated unique economic theories. The ANP advocated for a "collectivist society" under the banner of "Social Sanity," which rejected individualist capitalism . This platform included proposals for government-provided medical coupons, a guaranteed family income during economic transitions, the nationalization of monopolies, the abolition of the Federal Reserve, and state control over press and youth organizations . This collectivist economic model distinguished his version of National Socialism from other iterations and represented a complex, if still deeply racist, attempt to create a comprehensive political program. His organization also maintained a paramilitary posture without explicitly advocating for immediate armed insurrection . Following his assassination, the ANP was taken over by Matt Koehl, who transformed it into the National Socialist White People's Party (NSWPP) . Under Koehl's leadership, the NSWPP continued to promote national socialist collectivism and explicitly positioned itself as the "anti-system and revolutionary party of American youth" between 1967 and 1973 . The party's transformation was part of a broader effort to redefine its identity and strategy in the wake of Rockwell's death, including the adoption of the slogan "White Power" , .

The ideological schism that ultimately led to Rockwell's assassination stemmed from internal disputes within the party. By 1967, tensions had grown over what some members perceived as a shift away from dogmatic Nazism towards a more inclusive concept of "white unity" . This evolution, whether real or perceived by dissenters, created a rift among the party's leadership and membership. One of the most prominent figures to break with Rockwell was William Luther Pierce, who joined the ANP in 1965 or 1966 , . Pierce, who would later become a pivotal figure in American neo-Nazism, fundamentally disagreed with Rockwell's public propaganda strategy and his "Social Sanity" economic platform . Pierce sought a more clandestine, apocalyptic vision of revolution, rejecting Rockwell's model of overt political activism and electoral engagement . This ideological divergence highlights the volatile nature of the movement, where charismatic leaders could attract followers only to be replaced by those who championed even more extreme or different approaches to achieving their shared racist goals. The assassination of Rockwell did not extinguish the American Nazi Party but rather catalyzed its fragmentation and set the stage for a new generation of leaders like Pierce to emerge, leading the movement down a path of greater violence and insularity , . James Mason, another future leader of the white power movement, joined the ANP at age fourteen in 1966 and regarded Rockwell as a potential Führer, illustrating the powerful appeal Rockwell held for younger recruits despite the party's eventual splintering .

## The Assassination Event

On Friday, August 25, 1967, at approximately 11:55 a.m., George Lincoln Rockwell was assassinated in the parking lot of the Dominion Hills Shopping Center, located on Wilson Boulevard in Arlington, Virginia , , . The specific location of the attack was outside the EconoWash laundromat, also referred to as the Econ-o-Wash or Speedy Laundromat, which was situated within the shopping center complex , , . At the time of the shooting, Rockwell was seated in his 1958 Chevrolet, a blue-and-white vehicle, as he was backing out of a parking space , , . The attack was meticulously planned and executed from a distance. A gunman fired two shots through the windshield of Rockwell's car from the flat roof of the Dominion Hills Shopping Center, where the laundromat was located , , . The assailant used a German Mauser semiautomatic pistol, specifically a 7.63mm or 7.63×25mm model, a weapon that had been acquired beforehand for the purpose of the assassination , , .

The first bullet struck Rockwell in the chest, causing fatal cardiac injury or rupturing his aorta , , . The second bullet passed through the front seat of the car, either ricocheting off it or traveling through the empty passenger area , . Sources indicate that Rockwell died minutes later after exiting his incapacitated vehicle , . Some accounts describe him crawling from his car before collapsing near the right rear of the vehicle, pointing toward the roof of the shopping center from which he had been shot , . Other sources state he died instantly at the scene upon impact . Regardless of the precise moment of death, the injuries were unequivocally fatal. The location of his body was noted for its stark juxtaposition of the mundane and the violent; he was found splayed beside a box of Ivory Snow detergent and a copy of the New York Daily News, items he had been collecting from the laundromat , , . The entire sequence of events, from being shot to dying, occurred within a matter of moments, underscoring the suddenness and brutality of the assassination , . The choice of location—a busy shopping center parking lot—added a layer of public shock to the private, ideologically motivated violence, making the event impossible to ignore.

The minor variations in the reported time do not alter the fundamental understanding of how the assassination unfolded. The event remains a defining moment in the history of American extremism, marking the violent end of one of its most visible and provocative leaders.

## The Assassin: John Patler and His Motive

The man who assassinated George Lincoln Rockwell was John Patler, whose birth name was John Christ Patsalos , . Born on January 6, 1938, Patler was not an outsider to the American Nazi Party but a high-ranking officer and trusted member who had risen to a position of considerable influence , . Multiple sources identify him as a former senior captain, the No. 4 leader in the party, or its 'Minister of Propaganda' , , . He was also the editor of the party's official publication, *The Stormtrooper Magazine*, and played a key role in shaping the group's public image and messaging , , . Beyond his administrative duties, Patler was deeply involved in the party's ideological work. He was the creator of the white supremacist comic book *Here Comes Whiteman*, published in 1965, which featured a protagonist named 'Whiteman' who transformed via the phrase 'Lieh Geis' (Sieg Heil backwards) and battled caricatures of Jews and African Americans , . This background demonstrates that Patler was a committed and active participant in the ANP's mission before his dramatic break with the organization.

Patler's motive for assassinating Rockwell was rooted in deep-seated ideological disagreements and internal factionalism within the party , . He was expelled from the American Nazi Party in March–April 1967, a period of intense turmoil . The reasons for his expulsion were explicitly tied to fomenting internal division and holding ideological deviations from Rockwell's leadership . Specifically, Patler advocated for a coup led by 'Mediterranean' members against what he called the 'blue-eyed devils,' reflecting a belief in a hierarchy of white supremacy that conflicted with Rockwell's vision . Furthermore, he supported Marxist-influenced reforms and sought to reduce the use of German symbolism, pushing back against what he saw as Rockwell's increasingly rigid and dogmatic brand of Nazism . Another source notes that Patler's disagreement centered on Rockwell's growing shift towards a concept of "white unity," which dissatisfied purists within the party . These internal disputes created a bitter rivalry between the two men, transforming a professional relationship into a personal and ideological conflict that culminated in murder.

The assassination was not an impulsive act but a premeditated crime. Patler surveilled Rockwell’s daily routines from his own residence at 2522 Lee Highway in Arlington, carefully observing his habits to find the optimal opportunity for the attack . He then acquired the murder weapon, a 7.63×25mm Mauser pistol owned by another ANP member, Robert Allison Lloyd, demonstrating a clear intent to commit homicide , . On the day of the assassination, Patler carried out his plan with precision, firing from the rooftop of the shopping center where Rockwell regularly visited the laundromat , . After completing the murder, Patler fled the scene, discarding his raincoat and cap in a nearby yard , . He was arrested within 30 to 45 minutes of the shooting at a bus stop one mile from the scene, wearing a yellow shirt that matched descriptions given by witnesses , , . His swift capture was aided by eyewitness identification and physical evidence recovered from the crime scene, including footprints on the shopping center roof that matched his shoes , . Ballistics testing later confirmed that the recovered Mauser pistol was the murder weapon, linking Patler directly to the crime , . The case against him was built on a combination of circumstantial and forensic evidence, which proved overwhelming for the defense.

## Legal Proceedings and Sentencing

Following his arrest, John Patler faced a highly publicized trial for the first-degree murder of George Lincoln Rockwell , . The prosecution presented a compelling case built on eyewitness testimony, forensic evidence, and ballistics analysis , . Key pieces of evidence included eyewitnesses who identified Patler as the shooter and the recovery of his discarded raincoat and cap near the scene , . Crucially, investigators found footprints on the roof of the Dominion Hills Shopping Center that matched the soles of Patler's shoes, providing a direct physical link to the location from which the shots were fired , . Further evidence came from ballistics testing, which connected the murder weapon—a German Mauser pistol—to test-firings conducted on property belonging to Patler’s father-in-law in Highland County, Virginia , . The prosecution argued that Patler had acted with premeditation, having surveilled Rockwell and acquired the weapon weeks prior to the assassination .

During the trial, Patler attempted to present an alibi, but the jury ultimately rejected it in favor of the prosecution's evidence . The legal proceedings were extensive, featuring a record-breaking three-week jury trial with a transcript exceeding 1,500 pages . The court formally established that Rockwell was indeed "head of the nazi party in America," thereby confirming the significance of the victim and the political context of the murder . The jury deliberated for four hours before finding Patler guilty of first-degree murder on December 15, 1967 , . There are slight discrepancies in the reported length of the deliberation, with one source stating four hours and another mentioning 30 hours . Regardless of the exact duration, the verdict was a foregone conclusion given the strength of the evidence presented.

Patler was sentenced to 20 years in prison for his conviction , , . His lengthy sentence reflected the gravity of the crime, which was seen as a betrayal of a fellow extremist leader. Over the course of his incarceration, Patler violated his parole conditions and was returned to prison, serving an additional six years beyond his original sentence . He was eventually paroled in 1975 after having served less than half of his initial 20-year term . Throughout his appeals process, Patler never admitted guilt for the murder . He pursued unsuccessful appeals to both the Supreme Court of Virginia, which affirmed his conviction on November 30, 1970, and the U.S. Supreme Court, which denied his petition in May 1972 , . His unwavering denial of guilt, despite the overwhelming evidence against him, underscores the deep ideological convictions that may have driven his actions, framing the murder not as a criminal act but as a necessary ideological purge.

The legal outcome was definitive, delivering justice for Rockwell and cementing Patler's status as the convicted murderer. However, the case also highlighted the challenges in prosecuting politically motivated crimes, as Patler's steadfast refusal to confess suggests that his actions were viewed through the lens of his extremist ideology.

## Immediate Aftermath and Reorganization

The assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell sent shockwaves through the American white power movement, creating a significant power vacuum that necessitated immediate reorganization. With its founder and charismatic leader eliminated, the American Nazi Party (ANP) faced an existential crisis. The immediate response was a succession of leadership under the command of Matt Koehl, who took over the party's operations , . This transition marked a critical juncture for the organization, forcing it to adapt its identity and strategy in the absence of Rockwell's singular vision. Recognizing the need to move forward while distancing itself from the infamy surrounding the assassination, the party underwent a formal rebranding. It was renamed the National Socialist White People's Party (NSWPP), signaling a new chapter for the movement , . This change was accompanied by the adoption of the slogan "White Power," a rallying cry intended to galvanize supporters and project a renewed sense of purpose .

Despite these efforts to reorganize and rebrand, the post-Rockwell era was characterized by continued instability and internal fragmentation. The NSWPP, under Koehl's leadership, sought to maintain the party's core tenets, including its promotion of national socialist collectivism, but the unifying force of Rockwell's personality was irreplaceable . The party splintered into a number of smaller groups, each embroiled in denunciations and counter-accusations, a pattern familiar to observers of the extreme right . This infighting demonstrated that the assassination had not unified the movement but had instead exposed its underlying ideological fissures, allowing various factions to pursue divergent paths. The NSWPP, as the direct successor to the ANP, continued to operate, but its influence and cohesion were diminished compared to the height of Rockwell's leadership .

The assassination also had profound consequences for the careers of other key figures within the movement. William Luther Pierce, who had already joined the ANP in 1965 or 1966, emerged as a principal leader following Rockwell's death , . However, Pierce's rise to power was not a continuation of Rockwell's legacy but rather a rejection of it. He fundamentally disagreed with Rockwell's approach, particularly the "Social Sanity" economic platform and the strategy of engaging in overt political activism . Instead, Pierce began to formulate his own vision, which emphasized a more clandestine, apocalyptic struggle for racial preservation. This ideological divergence set the stage for the next major evolution in American neo-Nazism. After leaving the ANP, Pierce became involved with the National Youth Alliance and, in 1974, founded the National Alliance, where he could fully articulate his revolutionary ideology . The assassination of Rockwell thus served as a catalyst, clearing the way for figures like Pierce to reshape the movement according to their own more radical and insular philosophies. The event, therefore, paradoxically accelerated the movement's drift away from Rockwell's public-facing model toward a more secretive and violent future.

## Long-Term Legacy and Ideological Impact

The assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell stands as a pivotal inflection point in the history of American white nationalism, with a legacy that extends far beyond the immediate aftermath of his death. While the act eliminated a prominent figure, it paradoxically cleared the path for a more extreme and revolutionary form of the movement to flourish. The most significant long-term consequence was the ideological evolution spearheaded by William Luther Pierce, who rose to prominence after the assassination , . Rejecting Rockwell's "Social Sanity" collectivist economics and his strategy of public rallies and media outreach, Pierce championed a clandestine, apocalyptic vision of revolution . This new direction culminated in the founding of the National Alliance in 1974 and the publication of his seminal novel, *The Turner Diaries*, in 1978 , . Written under the pseudonym Andrew Macdonald, the novel depicts a violent race war that begins in the United States and leads to a global conflict, systematic extermination of non-whites and Jews, and the destruction of Washington, D.C. , . The FBI has characterized *The Turner Diaries* as "the bible of the racist right," a testament to its profound influence on subsequent generations of extremists .

The tangible impact of this ideological shift is starkly illustrated by its direct influence on acts of domestic terrorism. The most infamous example is Timothy McVeigh, the perpetrator of the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing, which killed 168 people , . McVeigh selected April 19 for his attack because it marked the second anniversary of the Waco siege, an event he perceived as a federal overreach against religious groups . More critically, his bomb closely mirrored the design and assembly process described in *The Turner Diaries* for an attack on FBI headquarters . At the time of his arrest, McVeigh was found carrying highlighted photocopies of the novel, indicating its role as a direct blueprint for his actions . This connection demonstrates a clear and deadly lineage from the ideological vacuum created by Rockwell's assassination to a real-world act of mass murder. The novel has been cited as an inspiration for numerous other terrorist acts and has sold over 500,000 copies worldwide, solidifying its status as a foundational text for modern white supremacist movements , .

In summary, the assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell had a profound and enduring impact on the trajectory of American extremism. By removing a leader whose public persona and strategic focus had provided a degree of visibility and structure to the movement, the assassination inadvertently facilitated the rise of a more secretive, apocalyptic, and violent ideology. The creation of *The Turner Diaries* represents the ultimate culmination of this shift, moving the movement away from Rockwell's overt political engagement toward a clandestine, leaderless resistance focused on systemic extermination. The legacy of this single event is thus twofold: it marked the end of an era defined by Rockwell's flamboyant leadership, but it also signaled the beginning of a darker, more destructive phase in the history of American neo-Nazism, a phase whose influence can still be felt today.

John Patler served an additional six years due to parole violation.
John Patler was granted final parole in 1975.
John Patler's appeals to the Supreme Court of Virginia (1970) and U.S. Supreme Court (May 1972) were unsuccessful.
John Patler never admitted guilt.
The assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell sent shockwaves through the American white power movement, creating a significant power vacuum that necessitated immediate reorganization.
With its founder and charismatic leader eliminated, the American Nazi Party (ANP) faced an existential crisis.
The immediate response was a succession of leadership under the command of Matt Koehl, who took over the American Nazi Party's operations.
The transition marked a critical juncture for the organization, forcing it to adapt its identity and strategy in the absence of Rockwell's singular vision.
The American Nazi Party underwent a formal rebranding.
The American Nazi Party was renamed the National Socialist White People's Party (NSWPP).
The name change was accompanied by the adoption of the slogan "White Power", a rallying cry intended to galvanize supporters and project a renewed sense of purpose.
Despite these efforts to reorganize and rebrand, the post-Rockwell era was characterized by continued instability and internal fragmentation.

The National Socialist White People's Party (NSWPP), under Koehl's leadership, sought to maintain the party's core tenets, including its promotion of national socialist collectivism, but the unifying force of Rockwell's personality was irreplaceable.
The party splintered into a number of smaller groups, each embroiled in denunciations and counter-accusations, a pattern familiar to observers of the extreme right.
The infighting demonstrated that the assassination had not unified the movement but had instead exposed its underlying ideological fissures, allowing various factions to pursue divergent paths.

The National Socialist White People's Party (NSWPP), as the direct successor to the ANP, continued to operate, but its influence and cohesion were diminished compared to the height of Rockwell's leadership.
The assassination also had profound consequences for the careers of other key figures within the movement.
William Luther Pierce, who had already joined the American Nazi Party (ANP) in 1965 or 1966, emerged as a principal leader following Rockwell's death.
Pierce's rise to power was not a continuation of Rockwell's legacy but rather a rejection of it.
William Luther Pierce fundamentally disagreed with Rockwell's approach, particularly the "Social Sanity" economic platform and the strategy of engaging in overt political activism.
William Luther Pierce began to formulate his own vision, which emphasized a more clandestine, apocalyptic struggle for racial preservation.
After leaving the American Nazi Party (ANP), William Luther Pierce became involved with the National Youth Alliance.
In 1974, William Luther Pierce founded the National Alliance, where he could fully articulate his revolutionary ideology.
The assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell thus served as a catalyst, clearing the way for figures like Pierce to reshape the movement according to their own more radical and insular philosophies.

The assassination of George Lincoln Rockwell stands as a pivotal inflection point in the history of American white nationalism, with a legacy that extends far beyond the immediate aftermath of his death.
While the act eliminated a prominent figure, it paradoxically cleared the path for a more extreme and revolutionary form of the movement to flourish.
The most significant long-term consequence was the ideological evolution spearheaded by William Luther Pierce, who rose to prominence after the assassination.
Rejecting Rockwell's "Social Sanity" collectivist economics and his strategy of public rallies and media outreach, Pierce championed a clandestine, apocalyptic vision of revolution.
This new direction culminated in the founding of the National Alliance in 1974.
This new direction culminated in the publication of his seminal novel, *The Turner Diaries*, in 1978.

Written under the pseudonym Andrew Macdonald, *The Turner Diaries* depicts a violent race war that begins in the United States and leads to a global conflict, systematic extermination of non-whites and Jews, and the destruction of Washington, D.C.
The FBI has characterized *The Turner Diaries* as "the bible of the racist right", a testament to its profound influence on subsequent generations of extremists.
The tangible impact of this ideological shift is starkly illustrated by its direct influence on acts of domestic terrorism.
The most infamous example is Timothy McVeigh, the perpetrator of the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing, which killed 168 people.
Timothy McVeigh selected April 19 for his attack because it marked the second anniversary of the Waco siege, an event he perceived as a federal overreach against religious groups.
Timothy McVeigh's bomb closely mirrored the design and assembly process described in *The Turner Diaries* for an attack on FBI headquarters.
At the time of his arrest, Timothy McVeigh was found carrying highlighted photocopies of *The Turner Diaries*, indicating its role as a direct blueprint for his actions.
*The Turner Diaries* has been cited as an inspiration for numerous other terrorist acts.
*The Turner Diaries* has sold over 500,000 copies worldwide, solidifying its status as a foundational text for modern white supremacist movements.

_George Lincoln Rockwell was the son of vaudeville comedians, served in the U.S. Navy in WWII and Korea, honeymooned at Berchtesgaden, founded the American Nazi Party, promoted White Power, baited blacks and Jews, ran for governor of Virginia, made it into a Bob Dylan lyric, was played on screen by Marlon Brando and was assassinated in front of his neighborhood laundromat while fetching a bottle of bleach._

On a Friday in August 1967, George Lincoln Rockwell, the charismatic and outspoken founder of the American Nazi Party (ANP), was slain, not by the government or some leftwing enemy, but by a member of his own organization.

The political ringleader who had achieved national notoriety was doing his own wash at a coin-operated laundromat in Arlington, Va., just across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C. A few minutes before noon on Friday, August 25, 1967, the American Nazi leader, whose presence had embarrassed the suburban community for nearly a decade, told the proprietor at the Econ-o-Wash that he had to return home for some bleach.

As the 49-year-old Rockwell slid into the seat of his fading blue-and-white 1958 Chevrolet, gunshots rang out from the roof of the Dominion Hills shopping center. Two bullets burst through the windshield. One struck Rockwell in the chest; the other missed, passing through the front seat. The car rolled into another vehicle as Rockwell crawled out of the right passenger door of the Chevy and fell out onto the parking lot, his box of soap powder and a copy of the _New York Daily News_ sprawled near him. Bystanders called police, but in minutes the flamboyant—and ordinarily well guarded—leader of the modestly sized American Nazi movement had died of a shot through the heart.

Within half an hour, Arlington police would arrest not an anti-Nazi, but a fellow Nazi—29-year-old John Patler, a Greek-American and former Marine from New York City. Patler had risen to the No. 4 slot in the hierarchy of the party faithful, most of whom lived in a fortified “barracks,” a swastika-bedecked old house across the street from the shopping center.

Rockwell’s father (George “Doc” Rockwell), reacting to the news of the assassination, said his son had always known he would die in such a fashion. “I think he would have liked to get rid of the whole Nazi mess,” he told a reporter from his home in Maine. “He was more afraid of his own people than people were of him.”

The American Nazis’ slain, hypnotic commander was born in Bloomington, Ill., on March 9, 1918. He was the son of vaudeville comedians who counted among their friends Fred Allen, Fanny Brice, Jack Benny and Groucho Marx. Following his parents’ divorce, the young Rockwell attended prep school in Lewiston, Maine, before enrolling at Brown University in Providence, R.I., to study philosophy. He soon dropped out and served as a pilot in the Navy during World War II. He then attended the Pratt Institute of Art in Brooklyn, N.Y., where he developed the drawing talents he would use to create Nazi fliers.

After launching a short career in advertising, George Lincoln Rockwell married and fathered three children. When the Korean War broke out, he was called up and stationed in San Diego. He left his family when he was assigned to a U.S. naval air facility in Iceland. There, Rockwell read Adolf Hitler’s _Mein Kampf_ and became obsessed with Aryanism and the worldwide threat of communism. In 1953, only months after his first marriage ended in divorce, he married an Icelandic woman and honeymooned in Germany at Hitler’s retreat town of Berchtesgaden. He sired four more children.

In the mid-1950s, in a move that would estrange him from his second wife and family, Rockwell returned to the United States and conceived the American Nazi Party. He moved to the suburbs of the nation’s capital in 1958 to begin his climb as a national newsmaker whose every public statement carried shock value. The literature his group printed on its own presses spoke of the “lie” that 6 million Jews were killed by Hitler, and Rockwell was heard to say, “Bring me 15 Jews and we’ll make Anne Frank soap.”

Rockwell’s violent rhetoric prompted a court-ordered psychiatric evaluation of him at St. Elizabeth’s Hospital in Washington in 1960, but he was found to be of sound mind. He later boasted that he had been arrested 100 times but never convicted by a jury. In 1966, when he appeared in New York City criminal court on charges of incitement to riot through anti-Semitic remarks, Rockwell wore a bulletproof vest. He’d been shot at before, and had unsuccessfully sought permission to carry a pistol.

From the beginning of his movement, Rockwell used a variety of publicity-generating tactics to spread his message of hate against Jews and blacks. American Nazis picketed Israeli Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion during his 1960 visit to Washington. That year, after New York City Mayor Robert Wagner banned Rockwell from speaking at a July 4 celebration in Union Square, the ANP picketed the White House. They demonstrated at theaters showing the 1961 movie _Exodus_, earning Rockwell a mention in a lyric by protest singer-songwriter Bob Dylan. The Nazis marched in front of nightclubs that booked black entertainer Sammy Davis Jr., whose wife was white, and who had previously converted to Judaism. Having established branches in several states in the early 1960s, the ANP was trailing and heckling the civil rights Freedom Fighters marching with Martin Luther King Jr. in the South. In 1965, the same year that Rockwell ran for governor of Virginia and garnered 6,366 votes, the California Justice Department investigated Rockwell’s West Coast followers for threatening violence. In Arlington, Rockwell’s grinning blond “stormtroopers,” wearing swastika armbands, picketed Jewish businesses and became familiar faces at school board meetings, where they protested newly enacted school integration. One flier read, “You can beat the federal race mixers.”

By 1966 his proclamations of “White Power!” made him notorious enough for African-American author Alex Haley to interview him for _Playboy_ magazine. (In the late 1970s, when Haley’s family’s story was made into the TV series _Roots_, Rockwell was portrayed by Marlon Brando in the sequel.) Rockwell told _Playboy_ that he foresaw serious race riots and that he planned to be president of the United States by 1972. He made an unsuccessful attempt to cozy up to conservative theorist William F. Buckley Jr. His Nazi associates presented their leader to Christian fundamentalists as a modern “Saint Paul.”

With his flashing eyes and 6-foot-4 frame, “Rockwell has all kinds of leadership ability,” said a 19-year-old College of William and Mary student who tape-recorded an interview with Rockwell at his headquarters in July 1967. “He never hesitates when he speaks, and he almost glows with confidence. It’s easy to see how he can use his power on ignorant people.” Ruby Pierce, an employee of the Arlington laundromat who was perhaps the last to talk with Rockwell, said: “He was polite and charming. He was tall and handsome and looked like a businessman.”

Some who grew up in Arlington in the late 1950s and 1960s have memories of passing by the various homes the American Nazis used as headquarters, most visibly the one that bore a large wooden sign reading: “White Man…Fight! Smash the Black Revolution Now.” As youngsters, they sometimes got their thrills by phoning to hear the tape-recorded hate messages delivered by Rockwell associate and white supremacist William Pierce, who would go on to write _The Turner Diaries_, a novel that in the early 1990s inspired Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh.

During the ANP’s presence in Arlington, there developed a division among residents and onlookers as to whether the odious group should be scrutinized—or simply ignored. “Most Arlingtonians disregarded them,” recalled longtime Arlington resident Jean Mostrom, who heard the sirens on the day of Rockwell’s shooting. Working as a census taker in 1960, Mostrom was instructed not to risk knocking on the door of the house set far back in the woods, which some had nicknamed “Hatemonger Hill.”

U.S. Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy declined to put the American Nazi Party on a list of dangerous domestic groups because he did not want to boost its notoriety. Similarly, newspapers in Germany, where memories of Nazis were still fresh in 1967, gave Rockwell’s assassination only brief coverage. Peak membership in the party probably never reached more than 50 to 60, according to John Rees, a Baltimore-based author of a newsletter on fringe groups. A few other reliable sources place the total hardcore membership at less than 200, although there may have been a few thousand unofficial supporters who helped from time to time.

Reporters assumed that many of the Nazi “stormtroopers” were actually FBI infiltrators, recalled then _Washington Star_ reporter Ken Ikenberry, and one putative member of the ANP in 1960 was actually _Washington Daily News_ reporter George Clifford, working undercover. Some reporters were reluctant to venture onto the Nazi property for fear of the reputedly vicious German shepherds (one of which was named J. Edgar, after FBI Director Hoover) in the yard. Yet Ikenberry said that when he and CBS News reporter Daniel Schorr raced to the barracks on the afternoon of the shooting, the dogs seemed timid.

The journalist who took the Nazis most seriously was Herman J. Obermayer, editor and publisher of the daily _Northern Virginia Sun_. In an oral history conducted by the Arlington County Library staff in 1987, Obermayer, who is Jewish, said: “The American Nazi Party in Arlington, I felt, was a terrible blur on the community, and that their activities should be fully reported. I always thought \[the Nazis\] stayed here because they were welcomed here. I really believe that if you \[had\] made them miserable enough, they would have left.” The three other daily newspapers, _The Washington Post_, the _Washington Star_ and the _Daily News_, all followed a policy of “quarantine” that attempted to keep the Nazi publicity hounds out of the limelight.

As he declared in _Sun_ editorials and in an article in the _Columbia Journalism Review_, Obermayer wanted authorities to investigate more aggressively whether the Nazis paid their business taxes and maintained licenses for their printing operations. And he spoke of a baby girl he heard had died while living in the Nazi barracks, which the commonwealth’s attorney never investigated.

One group of Arlingtonians who decided to take on the ANP was an organization called Citizens Concerned. In 1961 some 50 local civic activists began meeting to share information on the Nazis compiled by the Anti-Defamation League and the Jewish Community Council of Greater Washington. They were worried about Nazi indoctrination of local high school students.

Citizens Concerned eventually approached the commonwealth’s attorney with requests for public education campaigns and an investigation into possible Nazi violations of zoning ordinances. After studying the party’s articles of incorporation, the group approached the Virginia State Corporation Commission and successfully lobbied it to revoke the party’s charter. In 1962 the Virginia General Assembly declared Rockwell’s group an enemy of the state.

The financing of Rockwell’s band of underemployed and marginalized agitators has always been murky. But funding quite likely was one reason he chose Arlington as headquarters for a party that would eventually form chapters in Los Angeles, Chicago, San Francisco, Philadelphia and Dallas, as well as establish links to counterparts overseas. According to historian Frederick J. Simonelli in his 1999 _American Fuehrer: George Lincoln Rockwell and the American Nazi Party_, the struggling Rockwell depended on his mother for income all his life. Once famous, he made money from campus speaking fees. And he had some wealthy benefactors among far-right Christian groups in California and Dallas, although the Dallas connection may have been exaggerated. It also was rumored that he received money from Arab governments angered by the creation of Israel.

Yet another source of direct support was a Baltimore heir and white supremacist named Harold Noel Arrowsmith Jr., who owned a house in Arlington and lent it to the Nazis in the late 1950s. Given its unpopularity in the community, the party periodically and secretly shifted the locations of its headquarters and dormitory, each of which would play host to numerous public skirmishes.

During one confrontation, on the evening of April 21, 1959, Arlington police and the commonwealth’s attorney William Hassan, armed with a search warrant, raided a Rockwell home, finding a pistol, a revolver, rifles and 10,000 anti-Jewish pamphlets. Some 100 neighbors looked on as Nazis marched in and out of the home giving the “_Sieg Heil_ ” salute. Police charged various Nazis with disorderly conduct and maintaining a public nuisance.

In December 1965, the Internal Revenue Service locked the party out of another headquarters for nonpayment of taxes of $7,000. After the IRS confiscated their printing equipment, the Nazis moved their printing operations to a plant outside Fredericksburg, Va.

In 1968, when the post-Rockwell Nazis used subterfuge to move into what would be their final Arlington headquarters, a local dentist and county board member who was suddenly forced to share a building with them told a reporter he found the prospect “nauseating.”

Observers who glimpsed the inner sanctum of Rockwell’s headquarters were impressed most by the utter banality. New York City police investigator Tony Ulasewicz, later famous during the Watergate scandal, visited Rockwell in late 1961 and recalled in his 1990 memoirs titled _The President’s Private Eye_:

_What greeted me was a grubby haunted house….Clearly, this was no showpiece that would attract membership into Rockwell’s party. His glowing, published accounts of his party’s progress had been nothing more than a pack of lies. As I looked around, I noticed that bullet holes punctured all the walls of the house…I also saw a pack of unpaid bills high on a table. Rockwell’s electricity had been turned off, and he used kerosene lamps to light the place._

Disgust at Rockwell’s domestic habits was expressed even by one of his own. In a typescript memoir acquired by Arlington Public Library, a former housemate noted wryly that “Link,” as Rockwell was called, “as usual” took the largest bedroom. “Link would usually sit around and read or sleep away most of the day while the rest of us would work or look for work,” he wrote. “Many sympathizers would bring food over to the headquarters during the winter months, and Link would take the choicest food and hog it up and leave the scraps for everyone else.”

Following the assassination, the defiant and—to many observers—ludicrous behavior of the American Nazi Party was on full display during the controversial effort to bury the slain leader on August 30, 1967. Because he was a military veteran, Rockwell had won a Pentagon ruling that entitled him to be interred in a national cemetery. But military officials refused to allow his followers to use Nazi rituals, uniforms and flags in the ceremony. Although that refusal was challenged on free-speech grounds by the American Civil Liberties Union, the courts upheld the Pentagon’s order.

At the National Cemetery in Culpeper, Va., therefore, Nazis and Defense Department military police faced off in a six-hour “classic comic fiasco,” as reporter Ikenberry recalled it. In the end, instead of being buried, Rockwell’s body was returned in a hearse to an Arlington funeral home to be cremated. His ashes were last seen with his 33-year-old successor, Matthias Koehl Jr. The Nazis then held a memorial service at their Wilson Boulevard barracks, which drew some 30 admirers from as far away as Pennsylvania, Illinois and Wisconsin.

As the funeral fiasco played out, Rockwell’s suspected assassin was sitting in the Arlington County jail. His subsequent trial and conviction for the murder of the charismatic Rockwell would crimp, but not derail, the unlikely American Nazi movement.

John Patler had been arrested at a bus stop in a residential neighborhood a mile from the scene of the crime. Suspiciously running while wiping his head with a towel, and with his pants wet to the knees, Patler had been spotted by a deputy police chief who knew the regular Nazis by sight.

What was believed to be Patler’s discarded raincoat and baseball cap were found in a yard behind the shopping center, and his suspected weapon, a 40-year-old German Mauser semiautomatic pistol that fired 7.63mm rounds, was recovered by a patrolman from a stream in a park along his escape route.

In the run-up to the December trial, it emerged that Patler, who had been photographed standing with Rockwell at Nazi rallies, had maintained on-again, off-again membership in the party. A “swarthy, greasy Greek,” as one Nazi labeled him, Patler was suspected of being a Marxist, and he had also pressed to rid the American party of its German trappings. It was Patler’s idea to change the name from the American Nazi Party to the National Socialist White People’s Party, a switch that took place in January 1967.

After joining the party during its formative years, Patler had left in 1961 to set up a rival group, then returned a couple of years later. He had split again in April 1967, but a photostatted letter from Patler found in Rockwell’s wallet after the killing suggests that he again was seeking to reconcile with his mentor.

Soon after the arrest, one of Patler’s attorneys, Helen Lane, a controversial former member of the Arlington School Board and longtime Rockwell friend, announced that her client would plead not guilty. The commonwealth’s attorney sought the death penalty.

At the trial, defense attorneys argued that Patler was not among the four persons who reportedly were aware that Rockwell had left the barracks to do his laundry on that August day. Instead of being at the shopping center, the defense said, Patler—who did not drive—was three miles away at his home until 11:45 a.m. He had run errands with his wife and child, Patler claimed, and after he and his wife had quarreled he had gone out for a walk.

The prosecution reported having found footprints traced to Patler on the roof of the shopping center. Employees of nearby shops said they tried to chase the killer. A witness testified that he saw a man fitting Patler’s description running through the residential neighborhood a few minutes after the gunshots, and realized he was right a couple of days later when he saw Patler’s picture in the newspaper. Prosecutors also set out to prove that the murder weapon had been test-fired on Patler’s father-in-law’s property in Highland County, Va.

After a four-hour deliberation on December 15, 1967, a jury of 10 men and two women found Patler guilty of murdering Rockwell. Patler’s wife Alice screamed, “No, no, no!” He was given a 20-year prison sentence.

While still free awaiting an appeal of his murder conviction in 1969, Patler won a $15,000 libel suit against a Nazi official who had told the FBI that Patler had stolen the gun used to kill Rockwell. After losing an appeal to the Virginia Supreme Court in the murder case, Patler served four years at a prison near Martinsville, Va. He was paroled in August 1975, but parole violations would land him back in prison until the early ’80s. In 1977 he had announced he would change his name back to its Greek original, John Christ Patsolos. After his release, he reportedly went on to launch a Spanish-language newspaper, but after it failed, he became a commercial artist.

In his estate, Rockwell left behind $257 in cash, his trademark corncob pipe and various writings. His successor as leader of the party, Koehl, was even accused by some party members of masterminding Rockwell’s assassination. Koehl tried to further the movement but he was no match for Rockwell as a rabble-rousing speaker.

Newspapers in subsequent years would report sporadic feuds and even gun battles against and between Nazis. In 1976, during Arlington’s Bicentennial Independence Day parade, the Nazis marched with a swastika-decorated drum corps, and in 1977 some 30 to 40 antiracist protestors threw rocks and eggs at Nazi headquarters. On the 10th anniversary of Rockwell’s shooting, Koehl led a commemorative ceremony at the spot where Rockwell died, laying a wreath and painting a swastika on the pavement.

In 1982 an Arlington Nazi named Martin Kerr announced that the organization was changing its name to New Order and moving to the Midwest, later settling in New Berlin, Wis. Another Arlington-based Nazi, Harold Covington, moved back to his home in North Carolina and set up a Nazi training camp near Raleigh. He later ran unsuccessfully for state attorney general.

Into the 21st century, Rockwell’s legacy was being carried on by the National Socialist White Peoples’ Party headed by Covington, using the name Winston Smith. The group promotes and sells Rockwell’s writings and audiotaped speeches on Web sites. But when today’s Arlingtonians tell the story of their hometown, the name George Lincoln Rockwell is seldom mentioned.

Originally published in the February 2006 issue of _American History._ To subscribe, click [here](https://shop.historynet.com/?utm_source=historynet&utm_medium=nav&campaign=funnel).
